title: MOBI-INTEGRATION: Implementation of an Interprofessional (Early-)Mobi- lization Protocol as Standard of Care in a Neurosurgical–Anesthesiological Intensive Care Unit – A Prospective Observational Implementation Study incorporating historical retrospective routine Care Data
summary:
Background
People with an aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage—a severe form of brain hemorrhage in which a dilated blood vessel in the brain ruptures and blood leaks into the space between the brain and the meninges—are often treated in an intensive care unit. They are frequently confined to bed for extended periods in the intensive care unit. This can lead to various complications. These include muscle weakness, difficulty getting up and walking, confusion, pressure sores, or breathing problems. This can delay recovery. For this reason, early mobilization is already recommended as part of standard treatment. This includes, for example, sitting on the edge of the bed, transferring to a chair, or taking the first steps with support. These measures are in line with current medical guidelines.
Consequently, a standardized protocol for (early) mobilization was developed at the Neurosurgical and Anesthesiological Intensive Care Unit in Mannheim. It helps nurses, physicians, and physical therapists work together to decide when and to what extent mobilization is possible and what requires special attention during the process. This is not a new therapy

Research Question
The study examines how mobilization of patients with this severe cerebral hemorrhage is carried out in everyday clinical practice following the introduction of the standardized protocol. It looks at when a relevant level of mobility is first achieved, how early, how often, and to what extent mobilization takes place, and how safely mobilization can be performed. To provide context, selected results are compared with existing treatment data from the period prior to the introduction of the new protocol. The study also examines how patients experience their mobilization during treatment, whether they consider the extent of mobilization to be appropriate, what importance they attach to mobilization for their recovery, and how independent they are approximately three months after discharge from the hospital.
Another focus is on how the new approach is adopted by the treatment team and implemented in the day-to-day routine of the ward. The study examines whether it is perceived as appropriate and practical to implement, which components prove effective in daily practice, and which conditions facilitate or hinder its application. It also examines whether planned mobilization decisions are actually implemented as intended.
In addition, the study examines the extent to which the accompanying training and support measures contribute to knowledge, confidence in practice, and application in everyday work. It also takes into account collaboration among nursing professionals, physicians, and physical therapists, as well as the ability to reflect on one’s own professional practice in relation to mobilization. Finally, the study examines whether the implemented procedures and safety structures are also used in the long term, become established in the daily routine of the ward, and can be permanently incorporated into routine care.

Methodology
The study is being conducted at the Neurosurgical and Anesthesiology Intensive Care Unit in Mannheim. Eligible participants are adult patients with an aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, a severe form of brain hemorrhage. Participation in the study does not entail any additional examinations or treatments. Medical, nursing, and physical therapy care is provided in accordance with the ward’s standard of care, regardless of study participation.
Consent is required to participate in the study. If a patient is temporarily unable to make decisions for themselves due to their condition, the treatment team will assess their capacity to give consent. If the patient is unable to give consent themselves, a legally authorized representative may consent on their behalf. As soon as the patient is able to make decisions again, their own wishes will be taken into account. Participation may be declined or terminated at a later date without providing a reason. This will not result in any disadvantages for further treatment.
The analysis primarily focuses on data that is documented anyway during routine care in the intensive care unit. The study examines when (early) mobilization begins, what level of mobility is achieved, how often and for how long mobilization takes place, and how safely this can be done. In addition, key information regarding the course of the illness is taken into account. The mobilization trajectories are also categorized based on whether patients were on invasive ventilation for more than 24 hours or were primarily breathing independently. This is intended to account for different clinical baseline conditions and to expand the currently limited knowledge regarding (early) mobilization in cases of severe intracerebral hemorrhage.
Two patient groups are being studied: an earlier group from the period before the introduction of the MOBI protocol (Nov. 2023–Mar. 2025) and a group treated after its introduction (Oct. 2026–Dec. 2027). The existing data from the earlier group will be used to better contextualize the mobilization practices and selected clinical outcomes observed thereafter. The study observes care in everyday clinical practice. Patients will not be assigned to different treatment regimens. The comparison of the two time periods serves to describe and contextualize the findings, not to prove that any changes were caused by the MOBI protocol.
With their consent, patients will be contacted by phone approximately three months after being discharged from the hospital. During a conversation lasting about 20 to 30 minutes, they will be asked how they are doing now, how independent they are in their daily lives, and how they experienced (early) mobilization during their stay in the intensive care unit. Participation is voluntary. You may choose not to answer individual questions, and you may end the conversation at any time without giving a reason. Refusal to participate or discontinuing the conversation will not adversely affect your future care. If you wish, the conversation may be recorded for scientific analysis; this is also voluntary.
The treatment team is also being surveyed. Nurses, physicians, and physical therapists on the neurosurgical and anesthesiology intensive care unit can voluntarily and anonymously participate in an online survey four weeks, six months, and twelve months after the introduction of the MOBI protocol. The study examines how the MOBI protocol is being adopted, how appropriate and practical it is in the day-to-day routine of the unit, and what factors facilitate or hinder its application. It also assesses the extent to which the training sessions contribute to knowledge, confidence in one’s own actions, and the application of the protocol in daily work. Interprofessional collaboration and reflection on one’s own professional practice are also taken into account. Based on treatment data, the study will further examine whether the prescribed mobilization measures are actually being implemented in accordance with the MOBI protocol and whether the new procedures and safety rules are becoming established in the ward’s daily routine over the long term.
The data will be analyzed primarily using descriptive statistics. This will involve presenting, for example, frequencies, mean values, mobilization trajectories, and trends over time. The goal is to better understand how (early) mobilization is carried out in patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage under routine intensive care conditions, how safely it can be performed, and how it relates to clinical outcomes. At the same time, the study will examine how the MOBI protocol is implemented by the treatment team and integrated into care over the long term. This is intended to expand the knowledge base regarding (early) mobilization for this patient group and to support the further development of safe and practically feasible care.


Patient data is analyzed in a pseudonymized form. Personal information is stored separately from the research data and is accessible only to authorized individuals. Surveys of the treatment team are conducted anonymously. Results are summarized and presented in such a way that no conclusions can be drawn about individual patients or staff members.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage who are being treated in the Neurosurgical and Anesthesiological Intensive Care Unit at the University Medical Center Heidelberg – UK Mannheim GmbH and for whom documented informed consent for the use of routine data has been obtained for prospective data collection, either by the patients themselves or by their legal representatives on their behalf.

The same clinical inclusion criteria apply to the historical-retrospective cohort; only existing routine data from patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage who were treated in the same intensive care unit between October 1, 2023, and March 31, 2025, will be analyzed.

Patient interview: Same eligibility criteria as for the prospective cohort; proficiency in German or English; participation independently or with support; prior consent to be contacted and verbal informed consent obtained before the interview.

The staff surveys will include registered nurses, physicians, and physical therapists with completed professional qualifications, provided they were employed at the NCAI of the University Hospital Heidelberg – UK Mannheim GmbH during the study period.
Exclusion criteria:
In palliative care settings, as well as in cases of confirmed brain death or when the treatment goal is organ preservation, no further evaluation of mobilization-related issues is conducted, as early mobilization is generally not a treatment goal in these situations. Routine data collected up to this point are included in the analysis; such cases are documented and flagged separately. Patients or data sets are not completely excluded in order to provide a transparent picture of clinical decision-making processes, contraindications, and the application of the MOBI protocol under routine conditions.

Patient interview: Deceased (mRS 6); insufficient ability to participate in the interview; refusal to participate or withdrawal of consent.

Staff survey: No independent responsibility for patient care and/or no involvement in mobilization-related processes; refusal to participate or withdrawal of consent.
